speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would not have taken part in this debate were it not for the character which my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) endeavoured to give to this treaty. In his opening remarks he paid some attention to me and he stated that I had spoken and voted against the treaty of 1893. That is a statement which I could dispute but I will pass it with the observation that if I spoke and voted against the treaty of 1893 I had the merit, which after all is not a very high one, of consistency. I remember very well that on the treaty, not of 1893, but of 1907, my hon. friend spoke one way and voted the other way, and I will be very much surprised if, although he spoke against this treaty tonight, he will not end by voting in favour of it. The hon. gentleman tries to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds, but that is his own business and the business of the electors of Jacques Cartier. The important statement made by my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) was that this is a mere childish treaty, that there is no necessity for it at all, that it is of no consequence to Canada whatever, and he gives as his reason that France is such a rich country that she does not need to import agricultural products. The hon. gentleman told us that France produces enough wheat, butter, cheese and other such commodities to render her independent of importations from other nations. Is the hon. gentleman serious in that statement? Why, he has not even read the blue-book which has been put. in his hands and which gives the statistics upon which this treaty was negotiated. If he looks at his blue-book he will find that France imported in the year mentioned here, wheat to the value of 186,666,000 francs, or more than $27,000,000. And yet, the hon. gentleman says that France does not need to import one single bushel of wheat. Lfet me tell the hon. gentleman, further, that France imported flour to the value of 5,887,000 francs. But that is not all. If the hon. gentleman looks at this blue-book he will find that France imported oats to the value of 50,000,000 francs, barley to the value of 26,000.000 francs, maize to the value of 51,000,000 francs and other grains to the value of 25,000,000 francs. Still more, France imported horses to the value of 11,000,000 francs and eggs to the value of 36,000,000 francs. Now, it is true that France is an exporter of cheese, but France only exports certain qualities
and in one year she imported 48,000,000 francs worth of cheese. These are the real facts and not the fancies which my hon. friend has given to the House. These are the facts which induced us to negotiate a treaty and to try to obtain some advantage in the French market for the products of Canada. Then, the hon. gentleman told us that France would not take our lumber because she has large forests of her own and a most admirable system of forest preservation. That is true, and in the preservation of her forests France is teaching us a lesson which I hope we shall soon learn. But though France takes good care of her forests and has large timber areas, France is a large importer of wood. If my hon. friend looks at the statistics in this blue-book he will find that France has imported:
Woods, common:
Logs, round, not squared with or without the bark, of any length and of a circumference at the thickest end of not more than 60 centimeters, 3,218,225 francs.
Wood, sawn or squared, 80 millimeters in thickness and above 10, 156,375 francs.
Wood, squared or sawn, less than 80 millimeters and exceeding 35 millimeters in thickness, 59,447,765 francs.
Wood, sawn 35 millimeters in thickness or less, 46,502,530 francs.
Stave wood, 26,461,770 francs.
In all, France imported about 200,000,000 francs worth of wood and yet the hon. gentleman says that the market of France is of no advantage to us.
I did not say that France did not import wood; I said that she imported wood from the Black Sea, from Russia and other countries, but I said that I did not think we could send her any.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, if France imports wood from the Black sea there is no reason why France cannot import wood from Canada, and if we have an advantage in the markets of France then I think the French people will buy their wood from Canada rather than from the Black sea. It is because France now imports her timber from the Black sea that, having the benefit of the minimum tariff, we will send her wood from Canada. Then, my hon. friend stated that he had no confidence that in agricultural implements we could make any impression on the French market or that we would have any advantage a| all from this treaty. That is not the opinion of the manufacturers of agricultural implements. On the contrary they have been pressing for the ratification of this treaty, and my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture did not exaggerate this afternoon when he said that we had a good hope of capturing that market. Sir, this is a most important treaty. My hon. friend is convinced of it,, so much so that-

I am pretty sure that I shall not be a false prophet when I say that although he has damned it with faint praise, he will end by supporting it with his vote. I have but one word to say to my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong). He appeals for improved trade relations with Germany. I have no hesitation in saying to my hon. friend that for my part I am not satisfied with our relations with Germany; they are not natural or what they ought to be. But the fault is not ours. We have been compelled by the action of Germany to defend our own position, and we have succeeded. My hon. friend has told us that German agents are very anxious to open negotiations with us. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has stated that as soon as we have disposed of the present treaty we shall be prepared to consider the other treaties. But let me warn my hon. friend that if we make a treaty with Germany, he will have difficulty, not with this side of the House, but with the other side. His own leader has told us that he has agreed to the ratification of this treaty simply because there is a provision in it that it can be terminated at any time on twelve months notice. If it were made for ten years, he would not vote for it, because later on it might complicate our relations with Great Britain. Therefore if the hon. leader of the opposition and those who support him vote for the ratification of this treaty because it can be terminated at any time, my hon. friend from East Lambton will have some difficulty in persuading his own friends to support a treaty with Germany. * In my opinion, we should endeavour to push our commercial relations in every part of the world. We have opened our doors as widely as possible to British trade in the hope that at some time or other we shall have preferential treatment in the British market. But, Sir, I shall not complicate this matter. It is possible to have preferential arrangements with Great Britain without injuring our relations with other countries.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to speak on this question, but I wish to utter my protest against some reflections which have been made on the opposition side of the House in regard to the agricultural interests of this country. Some hon. gentlemen have sought to convey the idea that the farmers of this country are not in a prosperous condition, and that this government has not been doing what is in their interest. I wish to dissent from that. We know that the cattle industry of this country has developed at a marvellous rate in the last few years, owing largely to the way in which this government has fostered the English market, and we know that to-day . cattle are bringing a better price than they Sir WILFRID LAUR.IER.
ever did before in the history of western Canada. Indeed, never in the history of Canada have the farmers obtained such high prices as they are getting at the present time for all their products, whether beef, pork, butter, cheese, eggs or any other pfoduct. A few years ago, when this government entered into a preferential trade arrangement with England, the opposition criticised them on the ground that they were not getting any preference from Great Britain in return. But what did we find? Immediately after that preference went into operation, the British people bought very, largely of our agricultural products and paid for them a higher price, and they found that our goods were worthy of a better position on their market than they had hitherto obtained. The more they bought, the better they appreciated what we sent to them, so that our exports to England doubled in value in a few years after 1897, when the preferential arrangement with Great Britain was entered into.
To what other country can we send our agricultural products at the present time?

We send some to the United States; but so long as we have captured the British market, which is the best market in the world, and are maintaining a position of supremacy there against all competitors with the exception perhaps of Denmark in one or two particulars, we need not worry about our trade with other countries.
Can the hon. gentleman tell us whether we are getting in the British market any better terms than any other country in the world? Are we not all on the same footing?

That is quite true. We have no tariff arrangements in our favour, but we have the sentimental benefit upon which considerable stress was laid by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) a few moments ago in regard to the French treaty. There is in our favour the power of English sentiment and the appreciation of a people who are willing to trade. And that brings out another thought in connection with this treaty with France. It opens up a larger field and a wider opportunity for the Dominion of Canada in the matter of making treaties with other countries. There is something even broader and more important than the effect of this treaty on our trade with France. I believe that it will make Germany desirous of negotiating with Canada a treaty by which our trade relations may be improved, and I want, not merely as a representative of an agricultural constituency, although representing as rich an agricultural county as there is in the Dominion of Canada, but as

a Canadian, speaking from a broader standpoint, to express my appreciation of the treaty that has been negotiated with France. I speak as a representative of manufacturing industries, of which we have a considerable number in the county of Oxford. I know that there is a large industry in Ingersoll that is very anxious to have this treaty ratified in order that it may obtain the advantages that will come to it as a manufacturer of agricultural implements. This will give that industry the advantage of some $6 or $7 per machine exported to France as compared with the American manufacturers. And we know that the trade in agricultural implements now amounts to $800,000 practically per year in round figures. Under this treaty there is reasonable prospect of that trade being more than doubled in the very near future unless possibly arrangements be made by which the United States may obtain entrance into that market on a somewhat similar basis.
I am surprised at the attempts which have been made to belittle our preferential trade with Great Britain and at the efforts of several speakers opposite to show that we should cultivate the United States market instead of the British and other foreign markets. Why, the English market is certainly the best in the world, and we obtain the benefit of it as already intimated. And in connection with the French treaty. I believe that we shall also obtain from it a benefit even greater than appears on the surface in the matter of concessions to us on the exports we may send to that country, besides the better feeling which will prevail and the advantages given to us of buying cheaper the French goods which we require., If there is something we want to buy and we can buy it more cheaply, that is quite as much advantage to us as getting better prices for the goods we sell. Several hon. gentlemen opposite have spoken of the danger of our getting French goods into the country. Sir,
I consider it an advantage to buy cheaply something I want, and I look upon that treaty as advantageous which will enable us to buy cheaper the goods we require and give us better prices for the goods we sell. The government are to be congratu- I lated on this arrangement and the people of this Dominion will appreciate, and appreciate thoroughly, this treaty which has been negotiated with France and which I believe will be ratified by this parliament.

Did I understand the hon. gentleman correctly to say that there never was a time in the history of Canada when the cattle trade was growing so much as of late years and the farmers getting such good returns?
I said that the prices of western cattle were never better than today.

How then does the hon. gentleman account for this fact that whereas in 1896 we shipped out to England and all foreign countries 211,000 head, in 1908 _we only shipped 150,000; and that whereas in 1901 we got $1,500,000 for what we shipped out, last year we only got $1,300,000?
I would say that the mortality which took place among cattle in the western states three years ago, owing to the very severe winter, materially reduced their shipments.
These were not shipped from the western states but from Canada.

Possibly I would not have arisen to say anything had it not been for the somewhat extraordinary statement made by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. I was surprised to hear repeated, perhaps for the hundredth time, that worn out argument that we got a preference from Great Britain for the preference we gave, and the statement in support of that argument that we were shipping a larger amount of produce than ever before to Great Britain. Why, we produce more. Look at our great Northwest with its many million bushels of wheat going out and increasing year by year, how would it be possible that our exports to Great Britain should not increase? We are producing more cheese and more pork, how then would it be possible that our exports would not increase. Hon. gentlemen opposite talk about sentiment. Did you ever see an Englishman who would give you more money for an article or buy it simply out of pure love. I take an Englishman to be a man of business. They do not do business over there for the fun of it, but on business principles and I admire them for that. An Englishman gets all he can out of the preferential tariff. He knows that we cannot buy a yard of linen in this country outside of Great Britain unless we pay a duty of thirty per cent, or five per cent higher than it was before the preferential tariff was introduced. Do you mean to tell me that the Englishman would not increase his price by about four per cent or five per cent to the Canadian purchaser? Where is the sentiment? All on the side of the Englishman. Well, the sentiment he has is for his own pocket.
Or the Scotchman.

Yes, just the same as the Englishman. Instead of saying the Englishman, I should have said the people of Great Britain. Do you mean to say that



under the preferential tariff, the manufacturer of Great Britain or the exporter does not charge the people of this country more for the goods we buy than he did before. I have before me a document which to my mind proves the whole question. We have heard a great deal about the increase in the cost of living in this country. What was it brought about that increase? Why' we had to come to the rescue last year of our civil servants and grant them increased salaries because of the enormous increase in the cost of living. I was not surprised at these men asking for an increase of salary. The policy of this country has compelled them to pay more for what they require. Here is a table prepared by the officers of this government. There can be no disputing it. At any rate I am not going to dispute it. Let me give a few examples from that table to show the actual increase in the cost of living. And where does that increase come from, if not from this double tariff which we have? I know I shall be charged with disloyalty if I say one word against the British preference, and consequently I am not going to speak along that line, but I do say that I am not one of those who approve of a double tariff. I do not approve of a douDle French tariff or a double tariff with Switzerland or Japan or any other country. I do not approve of one tariff to fix the amount of money that shall go into the treasury and another to fix the price of the goods which the purchaser shall pay. That is what we have under the British preference. The minimum or preferential tariff simply declares how much should go into the treasury of this country on goods imported into Canada. But the general tariff fixes the prices of those goods to the consumer; no doubt about that. The British manufacturer knows how much to charge for his linen goods, for instance, for he knows we cannot buy from the United States or any other country except Britain unless we pay the highest tariff. The same applies to cotton and any other classes of goods. And we have the evidence of this in the statement. I would not like to detain the House at this time by reading a very large number of items, but I will give hon. members some illustration of how the cost of living in this country is increased and how this increase has been brought about under the double tariff which has existed for some twelve years:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is becoming a free trader, he has been complaining to-night of the duties.

Well, I do not think the Finance Minister should blame me very much if I did turn a little along the

line of free trade. I do not think that I am advocating a free trade policy when I say that if you reduce the duty on a manufactured article you ought to reduce the duty on the raw material of which that article is made. That is not free trade, that is fair trade, but it does not seem to be part of the policy of this government. Fair trade i& what the people of .this country want. I will undertake to say that the glove manufacturer to whom I referred wouM not so seriously complain of the reduction in duty, of the advantage given to the French glove makers in the markets of this country, if he got a similar advantage in his raw material; the one would balance the other. But when you make it harder for the man in this country to carry on his trade, I think you ought at the same time to do something to help him carry on that trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We don't need a treaty to do that, the man can do it of his own motion.

What is the use of this French treaty if you can do it of your own motion? I will tell you how the hon. gentleman tried to do it last time the tariff was revised, he actually tried to put through this House a change in the tariff raising the duty on this raw material, this kid leather, from ten per cent to thirteen per cent. That is the way he would do it by Act of parliament. I remember well appealing to my hon. friend the Minister of [DOT]Customs, whom I always found fair; when I showed him the various samples of glove leathers and made my appeal to him, he saw the point, and came down, and said: Well, put it at ten per cent; and it is at ten per cent still, although in the first issue of the tariff of 1907 it was put at thirteen per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That only proves how fair we are.

Fair when you couldn't help it, fair when you were found out. The hon. gentleman became fair when he 'saw there was no justice in what he was doing. He was found out. Had he not been found out and exposed, I have no doubt it would have been thirteen instead of ten per cent. Sometimes I am accused of being a high tariff man. I advocated a low tariff in that case and I felt justified in doing it. I believe in a low tariff when a low tariff is the best for this country, and when a high tariff is justified and in the best interests of the country I am prepared to support it. Reference has been made to the question of wines. I have the honour of representing a county that grows a very considerable quantity of grapes from which a very good quality of wine can be made. I feel that I would only be voting in the interests of my constituents by declaring Mr. HENDERSON.
that 1 do not want these French wines to come in at such a largely reduced rate.
In the interests of temperance as well.

The question of temperance I need not put before the Minister of Finance, because he understands that thoroughly. I do not think it will make much difference as far as temperance is concerned, whether the wine pays 25 cents or 15 cents a gallon. I am not opposing it on that ground, but on the ground of fair trade, fair play. The people of those counties in the Niagara district and along the north shore of Lake Ontario have invested very largely in expensive lands. They have planted these small high-priced farms out with grapes and are producing an excellent quality of grape. These grapes are being manufactured into wine and I say it would be unfair to these people now, after they have made their investment, to bring about such an enormous reduction in the rate of duty on wines, so that this country would be invaded by the products of France while our farmers are getting nothing in return to compensate them.

Mr. Speaker, hon. gentlemen opposite representing largely agricultural constituencies have said that they are bound to look at this question in a measure from the agriculturists' standpoint, and so, representing that very important class in the community, I have come to the conclusion that I should support .this treaty in their interests. The Prime Minister has pointed out that many million dollars' worth of farm products are imported into_ France with which country we are making this treaty. The last speaker (Mr. Henderson) thought there was no force in that argument because he said we were not sending any in there.
I did not say that. Mr. PATERSON, -and because of the duty.
Yes, that part of it.

And- because the duty was the same, there being no difference between the maximum and the minimum tariffs, therefore, to secure that for the farmers was of no value to him. Be tor-gets this point, that that is a market into which the products of the farms of other countries find their way to the extent of millions of dollars, and the government in negotiating this treaty want to secure for the farmers of this country that they shall have access on the very best terms that that country gives to any other country for these millions of dollars worth of produce, that is to place them on a fair basis of competition.
They had that before.

But they may change that at any minute, and on these millions of dollars' worth of farm products they may reduce their minimum tariff by treaty to another country which produces these farm products in competition with ours. What position would we be in then with this treaty in force? One of supreme ease because for every cent they take off the duty to any other country they have to take off a cent to our farmers. . Is that nothing? That is where we are, that is the position we are in, and in the interests of our farmers, I think I would assume a great responsibility if I should lift my voice or give my vote against a treaty which secures to them that advantage. It is admitted that some of the manufacturers will derive very great material benefits. Have hon. gentlemen opposite discarded all their notions of a lifetime that I have heard advanced in this House, that if you can enlarge your manufacturing' industries in this country you therefore enlarge the market for the farmers' products? Under a treaty that will give from $6 to $8 advantage to our agricultural manufacturers on a binder giving them the market of France, as against their American competitors, thus doubling the produce of our factories, according to the arguments I have heard advanced by the hon. gentlemen opposite time after time, the farmer is benefited as it enlarges his home market. What he wants is men to work in the factories, to be consumers of his products. What do hon. gentlemen, speaking in the interests of farmers, propose when they suggest voting against this treaty? What does the member for Prontenac (Mr. Edwards) say? He says:	Do not legislate in that way, what
does that amount to? What you want to do is, when the American charges you six cents on your butter, to raise your duty on butter from four cents to six cents and when he charges six cents on your cheese to raise your duty of three cents to six cents. That is the way he wants to benefit the farmer? What will that amount do? The American sends into Canada 473,805 pounds of butter in the course of the year, and this he says is ruining our farmers. What does it amount to? Multiply those pounds by 16, turn it into ounces and divide by seven millions, the number of people in Canada and it will be seen that the butter coming into Canada is one ounce for every man and woman and child in the country, enough to spread one slice of bread a year. That is the theory that we have set up against our policy of securing for the farmers of Canada the certainty that France, which imports millions of dollars worth of farm products, never can admit the products of any other country at
a lower rate than ours. But then there is cheese. We import from the United States 231.811 pounds of cheese and we are going to save the farmer by raising the duty from 3 to 6 cents on cheese. Calculating as we did in the case of butter you will find that the Americans send into Canada about half an ounce of cheese for every man, woman and child a year. That is the Conservative way of benefiting the farmer. The member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) can go to' his constituents and say: I voted down the French treaty. If they sav to him: Are there not some good points about it, he will say: Well I do not know, we did not get any advantage. Just fancy the idea of talking to the farmers that wav and voting down a treaty that secures for them entrance to a market that takes millions of dollars' worth of their products.
Does the hon. gentleman advocate it on bacon and other things?

Yes, I will take the whole list, but I did not want to make my remarks too long. Our farmers after producing every pound of cheese that is used by our own people -have over 160,000,000 pounds to export to other countries.
How much of that do they send to France?
They want to send *some of it to France and that is why we are negotiating this treaty.
The hon. gentleman misunderstood me. I asked him if he made the same remarks with regard to bacon and I asked him that because his argument was so oily.
The hon. gentleman spoke of cheese and butter.
And also bacon.
He will find that we produce as much bacon as we required in this country and that we exported some too.
We import over 7,000,-**000 pounds from the United States,

Oh, I know all about the imports and exports; it is my business to look after them all the time. The way to benefit the farmer is not the way the hon. gentleman recommended, but it is to ratify this treaty and get the best terms you possibly can in the export market for that which we produce a surplus of, and I think we produce a surplus of almost every agricultural product. And now, as to subsidizing the steamship line, I am not a prophet, but I do know as a business man that when you make transportation more certain, cheaper, and more frequent, you will extend your market as you" could not extend it in the absence of such facilities. It may not come in a day or it may not come in a year, but once that steamship line is established and you have better transportation and lower rates, then I am hopeful that our live grain merchants and our farmers will avail themselves of that market which offers to them the best terms that are given to any other nation. That is what we secure by this treaty.

I rise, not to discuss the treaty but to correct the wrong impression that the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) left upon the House and perhaps upon the country. We all know that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike) is one of the most extensive cattle exporters in the Dominion.
He said he was a farmer.

I suppose h.e is a farmer also. I understood the hon. gentleman to .say that owing to the climatic conditions in Canada we could not be successful in the chilled meat trade, but the hon. gentleman knows very well that practically all the chilled meats exported from Chicago pass over the Grand Trunk railway through Canada and go to England via Boston, which is a very much warmer route than via the St. Lawrence. In view of that fact how could the hon. gentleman possibly be under the impression that we cannot compete with the United States in exporting chilled meat, unless it be that he himself wants to continue in the business of exporting live cattle? I believe that we can export chilled meats just as successfully as the Americans can and I know that the climatic conditions are more favourable in Canada than they are in the United States for that trade. Every day we see train loads of Armour's beef coming from Chicago to Cot-eau Junction and the cars re-iced there and sent to Boston. If the Minister of Agriculture will introduce this cold storage system that he has been talking about for years, we can bring our meat from Winnipeg to the east, re-ice the cars in transit and deliver the meat in England just as well as they can deliver it from Chicago.

MEIGHEN (Portage la Prairie) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 53) to amend the Railway Act. He- said: The sections of the Railway Act which I wish to amend are numbers 254, 294, 295 and 427. Section 294 is the one which governs the liabilities of railway companies for damages in the event of failure to erect fences, gates and cattle guards and maintain them. Section 295 refers to the same matter. Section 427 is the general section which involves a general liability in the event of failure to comply with any of the provisions of the Railway Act. Read alone, section 427 would seem to be sufficient for the purposes mentioned in this Bill, but by reason of the specific language of sections 294 and 295, the courts have interpreted the liability of railway companies, under section 427, in the event of failure to comply with the provisions respecting fences, gates and cattle guards, as limited only to such loss as may be sustained through the killing of cattle by trains and engines. The purpose of this Bill is to amend all three sections so as to extend the liabilities of railway companies to all direct damages suffered by reason of their neglect to comply with the law. Section 427 is wide enough in every respect except as regards fences, gates and cattle guards, but in that respect it is held not to be as wide as was intended, and the purpose is to make the railway company liable in case of default in that connection as they would be in any other.

maintopic: WAR VESSELS ON THE GREAT LAKES.
speechtext:
For a copy of all correspondence, papers and letters in respect to the agreement between Great Britain and the United States for the maintenance of war vessels on the Great Lakes, including the agreement itself, the several requests made for permitting United States war vessels to pass the canals, and the outcome thereof, and a list of vessels which have passed the canals, with description and armament, the places where they are stationed, and the purposes for which they are used.
He said: I desire to lay before the House some information and facts so far as 1 have been able to gather them, with reference to the question implied in the resolution. I find that on April 28, 1818, a proclamation was issued by the President of the United States of America as follows:
Whereas, an arrangement was entered into at the city of Washington, in the month of April, in the year of Our Lord one thousand eight hundred and seventeen, between Richard Rush, Esquire, at that time acting as secretary for the Department of State of the United States, for and in behalf of the government of the United States, and the Right Hon. Charles Bagot, His Britannic Majesty's Envoy and Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, for and in behalf of His Britannic Majesty, which arrangement is in the words following, to wit:-
The naval force to be maintained upon the American lakes by His Majesty and the government of the United States shall henceforth he confined to the following vessels on each side, that is-
On Lake Ontario, to one vessel not exceeding 100 tons burden, and armed with one eighteen pound cannon.
On the upper lakes, to two vessels not exceeding like burden each, and armed with like force.
On the waters of Lake Champlain, to one vessel not exceeding like burden, and armed with like force.
All other armed vessels on these lakes shall be forthwith dismantled, and no other vessels of war shall be there built or armed.
If either party should be hereafter desirous of annulling this stipulation, and should give notice to that effect to the other party, it shall cease to he binding after the expiration of six months from the date of such notice.
The naval force so to be limited shall be restricted to such services as will, in no re-Mr. OLIVER.
speet, interfere with the proper duties of the armed vessels of the other party.
And whereas the Senate of the United States have approved of the said arrangement, and recommended that it should be carried into effect, the same having also received the sanction of His Royal Highness the Prince Regent, acting in the name and on the behalf of His Britannic Majesty.
Now, therefore, I, James Monroe, President of the United States, do, by this proclamation, make known and declare that the arrangement aforesaid, and every stipulation thereof, has been duly entered into, concluded and confirmed, and is of full force and effect.
Given under my hand, at the city of Washington, this twenty-eighth day of April, in the 3rear of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and eighteen, and of the independence of the United States the forty-second.

By the President:
John Quincy Adams,
Secretary of State.
This proclamation, therefore, brought into effect and made in every respect equivalent to a treaty, an exchange of notes that had taken place a little previously. It is interesting to find that the matter was first brought to the attention of the British gov-ernmen by Mr. Rush, the minister of the United States, who addressed a note, on the 2nd of August, 1816, to Mr. Bagot, to which Mr. Bagot replied on the 28th of April, 1817; and on the 29th of April, 1817, Mr. Rush accedes to the terms laid down in Mr. Bagot's communication, and the proclamation of the President took place thereafter, as the final act. The first fact then that confronts us is that in 1817 a treaty was made-I should call it that, because it has to all intents and purposes the effect and force of a treaty-a treaty was made unon the initiation of the United States of America between that country and Great Britain, which was in effect so long as that treaty lasted, to dominate, and control and condition naval construction and the maintenance of naval armaments on the Great Lakes.
' Needless to say that this supervened upon the war of 1812-14 and was intended to prevent any cause for collision between the two countries on the Great Lakes and also to prevent any oost of armament as between these two countries. It was a condition of that arrangement that all armed _ vessels which, at that time, were maintained on the lakes, were to be dismantled and taken out. We were to commence, as it were, with a clean sheet of water in all of that vast region and from that time onward, so long as this treaty lasted, that clean sheet of water was not to he dotted by armed vessels excepting under the limiting conditions of the treaty. As will have been seen from the limiting conditions of the treaty the armaments which were supposed to be possible were very small and insignificant. On Lake Ontario there was not

to be more than one vessel not to exceed 100 tons, and to be armed with not more than an 18-lb. cannon; on the Upper Lakes two vessels having the same burthen and the same armament, and on Lake Champlain one vessel not exceeding 100 tons and armed with a like force. This certainly was an agreement which was not only wise in every respect, as it seems to me, but was also exceedingly economical. Now, let us place alongside of that, for this treaty has never been disturbed and

The 'Wolverine' is a training ship belonging to the United States, not in the service of the state naval militia as the others are, and its duties are the drilling of the naval militia, recruiting, generally perambulating the lakes and showing the flag. All except the ' Wolverine ' are vessels which have been transferred to the naval militia on the Great Lakes and all have been passed up-most of them within the last few years -through the canals under the authority and with the permission of the Canadian government.
That would be state militia.

State naval militia. So that we have as a total ten vessels of 8,000
tons displacement, 30 officers and 549 men, as far as I have been able to get the number. There were several vessels, the names of which I read but the complements of which I could not find stated in the reports. There are 24 6-pounder rapid-firing guns, 10 1-pounder rapid-firing guns, 14 4-pounder rapid-firing guns, 8 3-pounder rapid-firing guns, 9 30-calibre ' A ', 1 30-calibre ' M ' and 6 colts.
I find that the 'Wolverine,' in the course of the last two years, has been visiting most of the ports of the Great Lakes, has been busy recruiting for the United States naval reserve, drilling, manoeuvering and generally showing the flag. This naval state militia is kept up in two ways. The states themselves make an appropriation

and the United States also makes an appropriation which is distributed amongst the states for the different stations and vessels. Something more has been done for amongst	the accounts 1
find these items:	For naval training
station, there was an appropriation in 1909, of $1,095,600 and an estimate for 1910 of $413,400. There was expended in 1907-8 a total of $1,939,611, as far as I can get at the figures. That was expended by the United States government in erecting buildings and equipping a naval training station on the Great Lakes. I find also that there was a coterminous appropriation by the United States for a naval hospital building, of $250,000 and that that building is now progressing. These then are the two contrasting pictures: First, there was an agreement between the two countries, absolute, in force until to-day, without a shred of correspondence, so far as I can learn from either country, looking towards its abrogation and yet under that condition of a solemn treaty and agreement, there is a very considerable naval force consisting of state naval militia and of buildings and naval training stations, hospitals and other things contributed to or maintained directly by the United States of America. I find from what correspondence has come down that the larger part of these vessels have gone up within the last eight years. Some correspondence was previously brought down to the House and from it we learn two or three things:	For instance,
that when the United States wish one of these vessels to go up, having come to the conclusion to lend it to the naval militia of a state, they make application to the British Minister who makes application to the Dominion government to take it into consideration and that the Canadian government in every case, so far as the correspondence that I have seen goes, have granted the permission and have done so speedily and with very little reserve. I notice that in 1907, when the 'San Juan d'Austria' asked to go through, the British minister refers back to ithe case of the 'Essex and says:
In 1904, the 'Essex' was passed on the assumption that the United States government did not contemplate departing in anv way from the existing treaty stipulations relevant to the maintenance of warships on the Great Lakes. It is presumed, therefore, that the Canadian government would, in the present instance, wish a similar condition to be made.
From the correspondence I do not find that any similar condition was made and the vessels were passed up on two conditions. One was that they should not be armed while passing through the canals or water-reaches of Canada to reach their stations and the other that they were to be used for training purposes. That is, no armament was allowed whilst they were passing through Canadian waters and the Mr. FOSTER.
general condition was attached that they were to be used for training purposes and confined to that use.
In the case of the 'Nashville' on February 15, 1908, what appears to be another step was taken, for we find the British Minister
says:
The whole question of armed vessels on the Great Lakes has been referred by His Majesty's government to the Imperial Defence Commission and His Majesty's government will further consult your government (that is the Dominion government); but pending results of the discussion, do your ministers, in the case of the 'Nashville,' see any objection to permission being granted?
The ' Nashville ' was passed through in 1909, and, it is said, received her armament at Buffalo after she had safely passed the dangers and difficulties of the canal passage. I do not propose to make any criticism with reference to this matter at present, but wished to draw the attention of the House to the existing staite of affairs which had not come to my attention until I looked into the matter, and possibly many other members of the House may not have been aware of it; certainly I do not think the Canadian public is quite aware of the situation as it has developed. I find that the state naval militia or naval reserve of the United States on the great lakes is of the following enrolled strength:

It may be that a portion of the New York militia is at New York on the Atlantic side, but I was not able to ascertain that definitely. Thus there is a body of men trained as a naval reserve, 1,649 in number, that would be available on an hour's notice for any work on the Great Lakes in connection with the purpose for which they are organized. Of course the United States maintains revenue cutters on the Great Lakes, but they are not within the terms of the treaty, and I cannot find that any larger number are kept there by the United States than are necessary for their customs work, nor do I find that they are at all formidable vessels.
If it was good policy in 1817 to mitigate the cost of maintaining vessels and de- [DOT] crease the probabilities of armed collision on the great lakes by a treaty between these two great countries, a solemn engagement to keep their expenditure within a certain amount and their armament and vessels within a certain limit, it certainly ought to be good policy to-day. I am not, of course, oblivious to the fact that great changes have taken place. An 18-pounder

then might have been a formidable gun, but to-day it would not be considered in a very high class as regards armament. A vessel of 100 tons was the same size then as it is now, and if all that -was required at that time was a vessel of that size, possibly all that is required for the same work today would be a vessel of that size. I do not imagine that the waters of the lakes are any more stormy or their navigation any more difficult than in 1817, and as there is no armed force threatening our neighbours in the United States, they did not need to have either heavier vesesls or heavier armaments in order to protect them from danger. But even if it be argued that the times and circumstances have changed, there is one way to bring about a change in respect to the subject I have mentioned, and that is for the two countries to agree upon the amount of change that is necessary and, having agreed upon that to modify, if necessary, the old treaty to that extent. But it certainly cannot be argued that so long as the same intention exists, and so long as the same treaty exists, either party would be justified in going beyond the terms of the treaty without first striving to have a new arrangement made to permit what they might call the improvements that are necessary owing to the progress of things. There has been a vast growth in wealth and in population since 1817. That is just where the importance and pos-siblv the danger of the position arises. I speak with bated breath in the presence of the coming Lord High Admiral when I say that I do not imagine that our equipment on the Great Lakes is at present verv formidable. I do not think that all the bristling guns and towering decks that we have there for the purpose of either defence or training have caused a shudder to run down the spine of Uncle Sam in the last few years, and so led to the extension of his naval defences and armaments on the Great Lakes. I am not sure that the little boat which we have there has a gun on her at all. I think at one time she had one, but it seems to me that I have heard a rumour that men were apt to injure themselves with so unusual piece of machinery, and so it was removed. However that may be, I am safe in saying that we have not been threatening our neighbours in that respect. Now, if population and business interests have increased, if trade has grown and great cities have arisen, on the Great Lakes, so far as the United States is concerned, this is also true of Canada; and what I want to bring to The attention of the House and to the attention of the people of Canada to-day is this, that as matters stand to-day in actuality, our whole lake population, our whole lake wealth, and our whole lake trade, are absolutely at the mercy of the armament which the United States has on those lakes to-day. I read the armament and the vessels; and if it did so happen, as I hope it never may happen, that difficulty arose, within 24 hours the whole lake trade, with all our improvements for the conveyance of trade, would be absolutely at the mercy and in the hands of the United States of America. If you take into account the relative equipments of the two countries on the lakes, Canada has absolutely nothing, while the United States has the armament which I have mentioned. While we may be all advocates of peace and may be all believers in peace, most of us believe in some sort of insurance, and if hostilities did arise between the United States and Canada, what protection would we have under present circumstances that would be worth a single rush leaf? We have none, and from the top of Ithe Great Lakes, where our great continental railways make their connections with the water, all down through the ports and harbours, with their docks and other equipment for trade, our canal system at the Sault and our canal system between Lakes Ontario and Erie, our cities on * the lakes of Ontario down to Kingston and the Thousand Islands, and still further our communications along the River St. Lawrence-all of these would be absolutely at the mercy of a force under the flag of the United States, which is quite sufficient to annihilate for the time being our trade. This is a state of things which evidently ought not to exist; and though we be the greatest advocates of peace and the most optimistic believers in peace, there is absolutely no insurance in that respect. No business man would put his business in such a condition of risk, and Canada itself surely cannot feel that it ought to do so. But a strange thing took place, to which I must refer. Although we have not had information in this regard, the government has had plenty of information, and that information has been collated and the Minister of Marine has evidently gone pretty particularly into It. He has made calculations and has raised a claim for non-participation in the naval defence of the empire by telling the empire, at the conference in London in 1907, -what risks there were to Canada and what a burden Canada had thrust upon her, and what a burden the minister had specially thrust upon himself, in order to safeguard our interests on the Great Lakes. I think it is well that I should read the portion that refers to this matter, although I read it the other day. Although no such information had been given to us in Canada, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries made this statement at the conference:
We have to-day on the lakes a boat which is an armed boat.

I can understand how the members of the conference pictured in their minds this contribution to the imperial navy, being used to seeing in the Thames the great 18-mile procession of warships, the armed boats of the empire. No doubt their imagination flew easily to the turreted ship or the armoured cruiser which the minister was talking about as a great burden economically and a great engine of defence.
We have to-day on the lakes a boat which is an armed boat, which is looking specially after the protection of our fisheries against the American fishermen, not only for the carrying out of the local regulations, but mostly and I may say almost exclusively for preventing the Americans from coming and fishing in our waters. We have on the Great Lakes (large seas, properly speaking) American states bordering these great lakes, and they are having navies of their own now. I think that three states bordering on the three great lakes, Ohio, Michigan and Illinois are spending not less than $15,000,000 themselves for keeping up a navy on these lakes,

One unit that Canada was asked to present would cost that amount, maybe a little more-
-and are drilling their men on the shore of the lakes. Besides they have some ships which are not on-because it would be against the conclusions of the treaty-but built in order to be prepared in case of emergency.
So that the minister himself there makes a statement tantamount to this, that we have been allowing these vessels to. pass through our waters provided they were unarmed, but with the perfect knowledge that after they got into the lakes they were ready for a case of emergency. My hon. friend says:
Besides they have some ships which are not cn-because that would be against the conclusions of the treaty-but built in order to be prepared in case of emergency. As far as Canada is concerned one of the first duties we shall have to look after is onr protection in connection with the great lakes. I may say that the wars we have had since 1763, since Canada has become part of the British empire, came from the "United States. We had an invasion in 1775, we had an invasion in 1812, and we had the Fenian Raid in the 60s. All those invasions came from the United States, so we have to look especially in that direction to protect ourselves, and I may say we have been doing it as far as the Great Lakes are concerned, not to a very large extent it is true, but to the extent of spending a sum of money which is quite important for a country of the size of ours.
It seems to me that proves a very thorough and complete knowledge on the part of the government of just what has been going on in the Great Lakes; and whilst we have been asking in this House for information, we have never got anything so full as Mr. FOSTER.
the minister communicated to the imperial conference in 1907.
It also shows that in the minister's opinion so great was the burden thrown on Canada to make proper provision for protection against possible enemies on the Great Lakes, that it was sufficient to put that forward as an excuse for not making a contribution or should be counted as an important contribution to the naval outlay of Canada.
My whole purpose is to call the attention of the premier to this matter and particularly the attention of the government. I do not say that it may be found practicable that modifications should take place on both sides as regards the keeping of armaments on the Great Lakes, but any armament maintained there should be in accord with treaty arrangements and not in violation of the terms of the treaty now existing. It may be that there is some argument for reasonable modification, but I do hope that as between the United States and ourselves, on these bordeT-line waters, consisting of the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes, it may never become necessary for the two countries to spend large amounts in vieing with each other in the building of warships. But the present condition of things is one which I think should give us some cause for reflection. When we look at the immense value of property along this line of Great Lakes and realize that, in contravention of the treaty, there is a formidable armed force on the other side and absolutely nothing on ours, that condition is sufficiently grave to warrant our making some move in the matter. What action has taken place I do not know. I am told that negotiations have been going on and the right hon. the Prime Minister may perhaps be in a position to give us more information than we have had up to the present. It may be that there are confidential communications, and of course I am not asking that confidential papers be brought down, but simply that we should be given such information as can properly be divulged and to which we are entitled, and if the resolution passes, it will pass with that understanding.

The observations of my hon. friend would have been more apposite if, when following the attention of the country to a condition of things which must cause anxiety to everybody and certainly to the government, he had been able to suggest a remedy. My hon. friend premised his remarks by stating that we have a convention with the United States since 1817 limiting armaments on the lakes. Under its conditions, four war vessels only are allowed in what waters are between the two countries. This agreement has been in existence nearly one hundred years and has served a very good purpose. Since the United States have reached their present

development, the states -which border on the Great Lakes, have been pressing the Federal authorities to participate in the war expenditure which has been going on from time to time in these states. The Federal government could not do so unless the conditions of the convention of 1817 were interfered with, and I shall not say that although perhaps they have not been absolutely maintained, they have been unfairly interfered with. My hon. friend knows that the tdnure of life of that convention is a very slender thread. It can be put an end to in six months time:
If either party should he hereafter desirous of annulling this stipulation and should give notice to that effect to the other party, it shall eefise to be binding after the expiration of six months from the date of such notice.
If the American government so desired, they could put an end to the treaty in six months' time. They could give that notice to-day or at any time. Under the circumstances, what are we to do? My hon. friend says we should have a modification of the treaty. That is more easily said perhaps than done. He may say put an end to the treaty, but that would be worse. In that case whatever armament might he established on the one side, we would have to. follow suit. My hon. friend will realize that the condition of things is one in which we ought to be very careful as to what we do and what we say; and I do not think that perhaps he has served as good a purpose as no doubt he had in his mind in bringing this matter to the attention of the country as he has done. It is a matter which has been engaging our attention again and again. When we were at Washington in 1899, at the time of the Joint High Commission, it engaged the attention of the two parties. There were mod^jpations suggested then but we'could not* agree, and the matter was left as it stood. Even had that conference resulted in an agreement, 1 do not know that it would have come to a conclusion on the point in question. There is correspondence of a nature that can be brought down and I shall be glad to lay that on the table, but there is also other correspondence of a confidential nature, but such papers as can be brought down I shall submit to the House.

That being the case, it must be that, the election protest never having come to trial, the judges did not certify to you, Mr. Speaker, the result which they found on the 29th of June last. However, whether or not that is the fact, or whether or not it is necessary under the Controverted Elections Act that it should be received, does not, as it seems to me, affect the status of the right hon. Prime Minister. Under the rules of the House, and under the statutes, there is no regulation in force in this country in the way of a time limit within which a member who has been elected for two seats must elect which he will sit for. Consequently, the matter comes under the provision of rule 1 of the House of Commons, which brings into force in all such cases the rules, regulations and orders in force in the British House of Commons on the 1st of July, 1867. Now, the rule in force in the British House of Commons on the 1st of July, 1867, was this: That, in case of a member being elected for two seats, he should, within one week, elect which seat he will sit for or, in the event of protest, that he should make his election within one week after the disposal of that protest. I would refer you to page 424 of Bourinot, where the rule of the British House is very clearly laid down. It is also clearly laid down in May, at page 652; and in May particularly it is shown that this rule which is now in force in the British House of Commons comes into force by sessional order at the commencement of each session, and has done so since at least 1842, and was therefore in force on the 1st of July, 1867. A case is pointed out in May where Mr. Daniel O'Connell, on the 24th of May, 1842, was compelled to elect as to which of two seats he should sit for. Consequently it has evidently been in force since the 24th of May, 1842, and was consequently in force on the 1st of July, 1867. Therefore, in the absence of any sessional order of this House, and in the absence of any statute, we must follow the sessional order of the British House, which was in force on the 1st July, 1867, and which would have required the right hon. gentleman who leads this government to make his selection within one week after the disposal of the protest, and after the meeting of the House of Commons. That is to say, that following the correct practice, the right hon. gentleman should have made his elec-

tion as to which seat he would sit for within the first week of this session. The first week, of course, is now past. The question of privilege, therefore, I have now spoken to. I had purposed, Mr. Speaker, asking for your ruling as to whether the right lion, gentleman is now properly withholding his election as to which seat he will sit for; but if you prefer my question to stand as a question until to-morrow, I am willing. But I do purpose asking for your ruling as to whether the right hon. gentleman can longer withhold his election in this matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: If your ruling, [DOT]Mr. Speaker, is that I must make my election, of course I shall have to do so at once. But I might give you my views; I do not know if you have any ruling to make on this point. For my part, I have no objection at all. I may say to my hon. friend, however, that I was particularly anxious to make a choice between Quebec and Ottawa, but so far no one in the city of Quebec and no one in the city of Ottawa has asked me to make a choice; therefore, I was waiting until I was prompted by some of those gentlemen who have done me the honour to elect me to both seats. But if I am not within the rules of the House, I shall have to put myself within the rules when I know what your ruling is.

CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT - INFRINGEMENT OF COPYRIGHTS.
speechtext:
LENNOX (South Simcoe) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 41) tto amend the Criminal Code. He said; A year ago, among the amendments introduced by the Minister of Justice to the Criminal Code, I suggested this amendment. At that time the Minister of Justice, after taking time for consideration, was of the opinion that the amendment was a good one, I presumed, at all events, he offered no opposition to it, and it passed. The amendment is to secure those persons who have valuable copyrights in dramatic productions against the unwarranted infringement thereof. At present they have no remedy except to bring action against the person who infringes their copyright, and as the person who steals the copyright has usually no worldly substance the aggrieved persons are practically without remedy. I am instructed by the parties who wish me to bring this matter before the House, that in many instances those dramatic productions are worth a royalty of $500 or $600 a night, and notwithstanding that a spurious imitation is presented to the public by some wandering troop, the head of which has no substance by which he can answer in damages, and therefore the party entitled to 26i
the royalty is defrauded of his rights and is practically without remedy. At the time when I brought this matter forward last year, not only the Minister of Justice but the Minister of Agriculture as well, who is interested in matters of this kind, were in the House, and as I recollect the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture at that time, he did not see any objection to it. But I must add that he also said that he had not had an opportunity of studying carefully the wording of the clause I introduced. I have no personal interest in this matter, though I think it is a matter of public importance. I understand that the copyright laws are defective in this respect, as well as in some other respects, and I offer this amendment as an improvement upon the law as it now exists. At the time I presented this amendment last year, the Minister of Justice had then, as an amendment of the same section, a provision in reference to musical competitions. That, I understand, emanated from the Minister of Justice himself and this was a further subsection to the same section of the Criminal Code. The subsection of the Minister of Justice with reference to musical compositions went to the Senate with this subsec-section that I introduced with reference to dramatic compositions. As you will recollect, Mr. Speaker, both of these amendments were introduced in the last days of the session, they, went over to the Senate and, as I am instructed, without any reasonable consideration, these two clauses were struck out.. I therefore move the second reading of this Bill in the hope that the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Agriculture will consider the matter, and in the hope, from what took place last year, that they will see the advisability of having this amendment again enacted and sent to the Senate.

I note what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) says and I can say quite frankly at once that I quite agree with his amendment to the Criminal Code for the purpose of dealing with dramatic copyright. I am not lawyer enough to say whether the wording here is exactly correct, but I believe it is, and I am quite willing to leave it to my hon. friend on the other side of the House and the Minister of Justice who says it is correct. My hon. friend is quite correct in saying that last year my colleague, the Minister of Justice, introduced an amendment to the Criminal Code in regard to musical copyright. I think it would be well therefore that these clauses should be incorporated

in a Bill independent of other amendments to the Criminal Code. I would like, before the Bill advances beyond the committee stage, to suggest -that a clause with regard to musical copyright should be included with the clause proposed by my hon. friend.

I would like t-o ask the minister whether in the proposed Bill any provision is made for stamping on small packages of seeds the date when the seeds were put into the package? This is a matter of considerable interest in the province of Ontario. For example, a wholesale seed merchant puts small packages of seeds into a box and sends them to the retailer. The retailer sells a number of the small packages during the season, and in many cases returns the unsold packages to the wholesaler. There is a complaint that the wholesale merchant continues to send out these packages, year after year, without any investigation as to whether any vitality is left in the seeds or not; and it is suggested that the wholesale merchant should be required to put on all small packages of seeds he sends out for sale the date on which the seed was put into the package, so thpt the farmer or gardener buying it would have some assurance of the vitality of the seed.

My hon. friend is quite right as to that point, except that the provisions of the Act cover it and more. When the standard of vitality is fixed, it does not matter whether the loss of vitality is due to the age of the seed or to any other cause. By the amendments to the Act, the percentage of vitality in the seed is fixed. In the case my hon. friend refers to, there are some seeds which are perfectly good for many years, while others are not good for more than one year. The average buyer is not usually aware which seeds are good for many years and which seeds are good for only one year; but the law, as we propose to make it, will require a certain percentage of the seeds in each package to be vital. In that way the buyer is protected better than he would be by having the date put on the package. I may say that in the discussion which occurred before this amendment was decided upon, with the seed growers and the seed users; especially in Ontario, where the seed commissioner met these people, that point of the date was not insisted upon or asked tor.
I can understand very well that those engaged in the seed trade would not ask for it.
I am speaking of those who buy the seed.

But the legislation of the government does not always meet the requirements of the farmers. The minister's explanation is satisfactory to those who understand it; but the farmer or market gardener would have to wait one year to find out whether there was vitality in the seed or not, whereas it would be a plain measure of protection to him if the date were on the package. As my hon. friend knows, these seeds are sold by every class of merchant: the druggist has them on his counter, and these people do not make any pretense of knowing anything about them. A child comes in and buys a package of seeds for five or ten cents and takes it to the gardener, who plants it. I do not see any objection to requiring the date to be put on the package, and I think it would be of great value and quite satisfactory to the purchasers of seeds. I am quite sure that many of these seeds are kept in warehouses for years until every particle of vitality has left them.

My hon. friend must not suppose that we have been discussing this matter chiefly with the men wno sell seeds. The representations that have come to us have been largely those of the association known as the Vegetable Growers of Ontario. Thev are the purchasers of seeds in large quantities, and they are especially interested in the seeds being right. They have not asked that the date should be put on the packages and do not think it necessary. I am afraid it would be a delusion rather than a protection. There would be nothing to prevent false dates being put on packages of seeds offered for sale. Of course, we could make that a criminal offence. But at the same time it would be almost impossible for us to prove it. No analysis we could make would prove that they had actually put the old seeds in. All we can prove is whether the seeds are vital or not.
The one would not interfere with the other.

There is no objection to doing it if there be any way of doing it which would be of use to the purchasers. The purchaser might think he was getting protection, whereas he really was not. I would not trust the date on a packet, but the testing of the seeds in the laboratory will show whether they are vital or not. If they are vital, I do not care in what year they were grown.

I am not referring to the case of farmers who buy seeds in large quantities, but I am speaking of the thousands of small packages sold in small towns where they have small gardens. A

merchant lays in a stock of some hundreds of small packages of seeds. At the end of the year he puts the unsold packages away to be sold the coming year. His customers are buying the old seeds, whereas if the Act were altered so as to compel the wholesale man to put a date on each packet, the consumer would know how old the seed was which he was purchasing, and would not buy seeds which had probably lost their vitality through age.

I am not adverse to the suggestion, and am quite willing to look into the matter. In the majority of cases at the end of the season, the packages which are not sold by the country store keeper are taken back by the wholesale merchant. There would be nothing to prevent the wholesale merchant from putting seeds taken from the package of one season into a package dated the following season.
Flow does it work out in actual practice? Suppose the seeds are sown after they have lost their vitality through age, how is the standard enforced?

The Act provides that any purchaser may take a sample and send it to the government laboratory and get it tested, and the results are li wful evidence in a court of justice. We prosecute in many instances, and the individual has recourse under the common law for damages. We always ask purchasers to buv their seeds long enough before seeding time to be able to send them to be tested and have a report back before th y are sown. If thev do not do that, it is difficult to prove the lack of vitality in the seeds.
Resolution read the second time, and agreed to.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the first time.
