FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved the third reading of Bill (No. 12) respecting a certain supplementary convention between His Majesty and the President of the French Republic.

Without wishing to delay the House, at this stage of the Bill, I would like to present a few considerations with regard to the treaty generally and also to refer briefly to one or two remarks made on the second reading by hon. members opposite. The Prime Minister and his colleagues laboured to show that this was a very good treaty in the interests of Canada and especially of the agricultural classes. Although I was not in the House when the treaty was first brought down two years ago, and had an open mind on the subject to some extent, I have failed to be convinced that there is strong reason for ratifying the treaty at thS" present time. I speak particularly from the point of view of one industry with [DOT]which I have been connected for some time,

fruit-growing, and especially the culture, of the grape. While, in British Columbia, we are not very heavily interested as yet in the production 0f grapes, in my old home district, the Niagara peninsula, this is a very important industry. There are at present about 18,000 acres in vineyards, the land used being expensive, with fairly expensive methods of cultivation involving some years before any results are obtained.
I remember when, in 1883-86, the grape-growers, of whom I was one, were fortunate enough to get from eight cents to ten cents per pound for their crop. Naturally, this price decreased as the area of cultivation was extended, until, in 1890, the price obtainable was only about four cents gradually decreasing to less than a cent and a half. At these figures, it was problematical whether there would he any return to the grower. It was at this time that the wine-making industry was inaugurated, improving the market and affording relief to the growers. Another assistance to the growers was the establishment of the canning industry. The effect of these new industries was to steady the whole market for our fruits by relieving congestion and taking care of what would otherwise have been a surplus product. The result was better prices for the product and a stimulus to the industry generally. So far as the grapegrowing industry in Ontario is concerned, the effect of this treaty must be to unsettle the minds of those embarked in this wine industry. In the fruit district in which I lived, one manufacturer was crushing from 400 to 600 tons of grapes every season. It can easily be understood what a relief it would be to the growers to have such a market for their product. As I understand the matter, these wine-producers apprehend that the lighter wines of France, those under twenty per cent proof spirit on which the duty is reduced, will have the effect of increasing the competition with not the most desirable class of French wines. Feeling that, as I believe they have ground to feel, they believe that the treaty is not a good one for this country as it affects the grape-growers. And the same may be said to some extent in regard to the canning industry especially as regards vegetables.
Now, I wish to refer to one or two things that were said in the debate yesterday. So far as I can find out, the attitude taken by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. - Monk) may, to some extent, be the true one. That hon. member says that this treaty is neither good nor bad; it does not offer any great advantages nor does it involve any serious disadvantages. But I understand that it is to cost, indirectly, something like $200,000 a year-that is, in subsidy to a line of steamshins. They also indulged in heavy expenditures for our plenipotentiaries when they went at great expense to this country to put that treaty
through. I have been unable to see that the cost in connection with * these two matters will not far more than outweigh any monetary benefit we will gain under the treaty. If we come to some of the remarks that were made by the Minister of Customs yesterday in pointing out some of the expected benefits, they were effectually dispelled, so far as cattle are concerned, by the hon. member for St. Lawrence Division, Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike), who stated that Canada could not expect to get any benefit from trade with France in respect to our cattle. So out goes from the argument one of the chief benefits which we were told would come to us from this treaty. If there was one part of that treaty which seemed to promise us any benefit, it might be in fat cattle. But here again we find that little consideration has also been knocked out by the supplementary treaty. I think, however, that my hon. friends opposite have themselves been the prodigal sons and have sacrificed the fatted calf in this respect on behalf of the French government.
Now let me refer to another matter. I was much struck with the speech of my right hon. friend the first minister. He addressed himself to the argument of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), who had said that in the main France was a self-supporting country, and being largely agricultural she would not therefore require many of our agricultural products. If I understand the right hon gentleman aright, he gave us to understand that France was the very reverse of such a country, and the fact that she imported such an enormous amount of agricultural products was a proof that she would becpme a most valuable market for our agriculturists. Now, if the right hon. gentleman will allow me to say it, I think his remarks were rather disingenuous, because while it is true that he was careful to speak of the imports of France-and I do not dispute his figures -he forgot to make any mention of her exports, which would put a different face on the whole situation. Let me take up one or two items. I will take an item which my hon. friend the Minister of Customs spread himself over, and that is butter. It is perfectly true, as he said, that large quantities of butter are imported into France. But far from that fact promising us a heavy market in France for our butter, I think the contrary will be the' case. Now, I am not quoting from last year's imports into France, but I have before me the Statistical Abstract published by the British government, covering each year from 1896 to 1906. I find that while France, in 1906, imported actually 15,964,000 francs worth of butter, she exported in the same year 53 972.000 francs worth of butter.
Now I will take up the question of eggs. It is rather astonishing to me to infer from * the First Minister's remarks that the

French hen was by no means equal to the occasion, that she was not laying enough eggs to supply the French people, and the Canadian hen, therefore, would find lots of room for her products in that market. I think the first minister stated that about 6,000,000 francs worth of eggs were imported into France. Well, in 1906 I find no entry of the import of eggs, tout when I turn to her exports of eggs, I find that France in that same year exported 14,720,000 francs worth. I might go on and follow down this table and deal with eggs, fruit, vegetables and things of that kind, which would show similar results. When we come to the item of potatoes, I find that France although no figure is given here of imports, exported 28,000,000 francs worth in 1906. She also exported 12,000,000 francs worth of fruit and vegetables over and above the value of her imports in those lines. I think the House will at all events get some clear idea of the nature of the first minister's argument, and will agree that it was rather misleading. We might have assumed that France was importing much in excess of what she was exporting, and that therefore we would find a ready market for our agricultural products in her market, whereas the contrary is evidently the case. In the markets of Great Britain you will find that France js our most serious competitor in respect of many of those articles. No member of the government will attempt to argue that France offers us a better market for grain than the world's great market where we all have to meet each other on an equal footing. France does not give any inducement or any lower tariff to Canadian grain.
There was another thing which struck m3 as rather strange. The first minister took occasion to animadvert on the attitude of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) when he said that my hon friend had been doing a great deal of talking against the French treaty, and yet he was perfectly sure that he would vote for it. But surely the first minister is the last gentleman in the world who should find fault with people who talk a long time one way and then vote another way. When we look at the hon. gentleman's career, and remember that in 1896 he talked for two or three months steadily in one direction and then voted in exactly the opposite direction, and when we remember how often since 1896 up to 1909 he has voted and acted contrary to his previously expressed principles, we must admit that he is not in a position to criticise my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier. It does seem strange to me that the Minister of Customs, who in stentorian tones-I think that is the proper word-previously to 1896 almost shouted himself hoarse in advocating free trade if possible, is now shouting himself hoarse in exactly the opposite direction.

It is an extraordinary thing, and I will be only too glad if, when they come to speak to the farmers in connection with this treaty, they will make some effort to show what they mean by free trade. In 1906, when they were talking about revising the tariff, a large meeting of farmers in Toronto expressed their views to the government on tariff matters. I find here a little article in the official organ of the Liberal party, the Toronto ' Globe ':
The memorial declares a genuine alarm, at the aggressive campaign of the protected interests, cites the promise that protection was to be only a temporary aid to allow the manufacturers to secure a foothold, and points out in contrast the continuous demand of the full grown and even gigantic industries for greater favours. It is argued that the protection accorded by the tariff enables manufacturers of certain classes of agricultural implements to charge Canadian consumers 25 per cent more than the value of the articles, and permits an overcharge of from 30 per cent to nearly 50 per cent on the cheaper lines of farm carriages.
I must say that one of the most singular phenomena, I think, in the whole history of our trade matters and our fiscal matters in Canada is the fact that gentlemen like my hon. friend the Minister of Customs who, as I say, talks himself hoarse previous to 1896 saying that he was going to abolish all these things, now stands up in this House to speak on behalf of those who are protected at the rate of thirty and even thirty-five per cent. This is the position that I find in connection with this treaty, and I have to apologize for taking up so much of the time of the House. I do not believe the treaty will be any good when it goes into operation, but I do believe that in some degree it will do a certain amount of injury to the agricultural classes, and that is the explanation of my complaint against it.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The particular point with which my hon. friend (Mr. Burrell) began his speech, that is the objection of the grape growing industry, was very fully considered when this treaty was before the House in its earlier stages. I remember that a deputation of gentlemen representing that very important industry came down to Ottawa and were heard at very great length. It was not unnatural that they should be somewhat anxious about that particular part of the treaty to which my hon. friend refers. I remember that when the treaty of 1893 was adopted by the House there was similar alarm on the part of the grape growers of the country; yet, I think that experience has shown that they probably did not suffer anything like the injury that they had anticipated. I will not undertake to speak for the grape growers, but I think I am justi-

fied in saying that the full discussion of the question that took place at that time tended to relieve their anxiety. They made at the same time one or two suggestions as to advantages which they thought might properly be conceded to them, to relieve them of what they thought might be an embarrassment and a disadvantage. Their suggestions in that direction were very carefully considered. Although the moment for action has not yet arrived I think I can safely say, as to one particular thing which they desired, that there is every disposition on the part of the government to meet them and that we anticipate that by the time this treaty is finally dealt with in such form as to make it effective such concessions will be granted to the grape growers or the wine makers-probably I should say the wine makers, although both interests are very closely identified-as will make them reasonably satisfied, and I anticipate that we shall not hear any serious complaints from them.

I understood the minister to say that experience had demonstrated that the treaty had not done them any harm. Have there been any importations of wine under the original treaty sinpe we discussed the question two years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The explanation is to be found in the fact that Canada is not a wine drinking country. The fear that large quantities of these French wines would come in was expressed when the treaty of 1893 was before the House, and yet I think statistics will show that the importation of these wines did not greatly increase. I have no doubt that we will have the same experience under this treaty. Our friends the French are producers of wines and naturally they will ask in making a treaty that regard shall be had to the things which are their particular specialties. Whilst they asked for some concession on wines we felt that we might give to them that, but at the same time we frankly told them that Canada is not a great wine growing country, nor a wine consuming country to any large degree.
Was that concession greater than they had under the treaty of 1893?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I presented the figures when the treaty was up for discussion and they will show as to that, but my recollection is that there was no very material increase in the consumption of the light French wines. Even though the treaty did give them some advantage our people are not a wine drinking people to any great extent. There may be some increase; if it were not so I suppose the French people would not have desired it. But, I do not think there is going to be any alarming increase in the drinking of wines because of this treaty. If our people want to drink they will drink other things which perhaps are not so good for them as these light wines would be.
But, the argument for this treaty may be put in a rather brief form. Suppose we begin by asking ourselves: Is it desirable that we should have a commercial treaty with France? I am sure there is hardly a member of the House who will sav 'no' to that proposition. Almost every member who addressed the House, while taking exception to some particular part of ihe treaty, said: Surely, we want a treaty with France. Let us assume that that is unanimously agreed to or nearly so; are we satisfied that the present treaty is sufficient? Any hon. gentleman who will give the matter his careful consideration must reach the conclusion that the old treaty, which may have had some good qualities, which was a step in the right direction, was a very incomplete and unsatisfactory treaty and that if we desired to have a treaty with France it should be a broader one than the old treaty of 1893. The world has moved since that period. I am not attacking the treaty of 1893, I am not finding any fault with it, I am simply pointing out that whatever may have been its value since that time circumstances have changed and it fails to meet the conditions of the present day. It we ivant a new treaty we must learn to give and take. It is the easiest thing in the world to say: Why did you not do this, and why did you not get that? Anybody who has to do with bargaining in any way knows that it takes two to make a bargain, and I think that would be a reasonable view to take in reference to this question, and that we should ask ourselves if the Canadian government, by making every reasonable effort, have been able to secure such concessions as seem to promise now or in the future some advantage to Canadian trade. I might put it to a test in this way: Would anv hon. gentleman stop and think and ask himself what article of Canadian output,* in the way of agricultural produce, or the produce of our factories, or our mines, or the sea, would he desire to see sent to France which is not included in the treaty? Although hon. gentlemen may think there are things in the treaty which are not of great value, it will be difficult, I think, for any hon. gentleman, who will give the question careful attention, to name an article which Canada is now exporting that is not included in the treaty. If that be true then I think it is not unreasonable to believe
What about fatted cattle?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I say to my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) frankly that while we

thought it desirable that cattle should be included we were by no means sure that we were going to do a great trade in that, and when I found that a small concession upon that point would be the means of disarming hostility in the French Senate I had to ask the question: Is this privilege a valuable one? I made the most careful inquiry I could make, from my hon. friend from St. Lawrence, Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike)-though I did not come into immediate touch with him-and I ascertained that that gentleman, from his own personal experience, was able to certify that the privilege of selling fatted cattle in France was not a valuable privilege, and was one, which, if given to us under the treaty, we were not likely to exercise. Therefore, we were making a concession which served a very excellent purpose from the point of view of our French friends, but which from the point of view of Canada was not of very great importance.
I would like to ask my hon. friend if he could name a list of articles produced upon the Canadian farm in which the trade with France will increase because of this treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not going to boast of that. The worst that can be said of these things is that we get the privilege of the treaty for them. If we cannot do any business in that line nobody is hurt.
Now, hon. gentlemen call our attention to the fact, and dwell upon it, that we put grain in the treaty-that we have the benefit of the minimum tariff on grain. But they say there is no minimum tariff on grain in France and some ungenerous soul said that you are humbugging the people, you are conveying the impression that you are getting a concession on grain when you are getting none at all. That is a very short sighted view of the situation. Suppose we had not put grain on the list. France would have been free to enter into an arrangement with the United States and give them a concession on grain and would have been free to deny it to Canada. And so we stipulated that although we sget no concession to-day grain should be put on the list in order that if at any time France should grant a concession on that article to any country in the wide world, she must also give it to Canada. Is that not something of value to us? Suppose we had proceeded differently. Suppose we had left grain out of the matter altogether, and suppose a year later our enterprising American brethren should make a new treaty-and they are trying to make a treaty now-in which they obtained a lower rate on their grain than we had on Canadian grain entering France, every hon. gentlemen opposite would have stood up and said: What, were these men about, why had they not Mr. FIELDING.
sense enough to foresee that condition and guard against it? We happily did see it and guarded against it. It gives us no concession for the moment, it does not give any advantage, the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Burrell) is quite right in saying that on grain we are not getting more than any other country is going to get. Sir, no nation, least of all a great nation like France, will give to any country a monoply of its trade. All that any country can expect to get is the agreement that at any time she shall not be placed at a disadvantage as compared with any other country. That guarantee we have secured as respects the articles mentioned in the treaty. But there is another consideration of great importance which has not been referred to in the recent discussion. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) said it was very desirable that Canada should make many treaties of commerce with the nations of the world. My hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) specialized. He said:	You ought not to mind this
French treaty but ought to make a large, liberal treaty with Germany. I shall not stop to say whether he was right or wrong. The reasons why we dealt with France and did not for the moment deal with Germany are well understood. I hope we will yet be able, in due course, to deal with Germany. But I wish to point out the effect of the various criticisms that have been offered. Suppose we had taken the view of the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) had agreed to make a treaty with Germany and granted certain concessions in our markets to Germany, I wonder if my hon. friend is aware that we would then have been obliged to give every concession thus granted to Germany to France without any return at all? There is in the old treaty of 1893 a provision-again I say I am not finding fault with it, at the time it may have been the best for the moment-which is the strongest justification of our making a new treaty. The old treaty of 1893 contains this clause:
Any commercial advantage granted by Canada to any third power, especially in tariff matters, shall be enjoyed fully by France, Algeria, and the French colonies.
Observe the wording, ' any commercial advantage.' That was not a reciprocal privilege. There is no clause in- that treaty which says that any commercial advantage granted by France to any foreign country shall be granted to Canada. There is a condition in it that if any commercial advantage be granted by France as respects the small list-and it was a very small list -of articles mentioned, to any other country, then on the items in that small list, Canada should get an equal advantage. But for all the thousand and one things outside of that small list, France was left free to discriminate against Canada. But:

Any commercial advantage granted by Canada to any third power especially in tariff matters shall be'enjoyed fully by Prance, Algeria and the French colonies.
My hon. friends will see that while that clause remained in the treaty unrepealed, while that treaty remained outstanding- and it is outstanding and in operation today-if we had made a treaty with Germany as suggested by the hon. member for East Lambton, every concession that we granted to Germany in that treaty we would be obliged to give to France- and we would get nothing in return. The argument of my hon. friend for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) was deeper and wider. He said it was desirable that we should make treaties with all the nations. Very well, the more treaties you make the stronger my argument becomes. If you had made a' treaty with Germany, with Belgium, with Italy, with the United States, with any country in the world, then whatever advantage you gave to that country in the markets of Canada, for compensation which might have been adequate, you would be obliged to give to France without any compensation at all. That is the position to-day and is the strongest argument that this old treaty should be got rid of. We went to the French government and said:	That is not a fair deal, that is
not reciprocity; you give us favoured-nation treatment upon a few small items, and ye, in return, have been obliged to give you favoured-nation treatment upon the whole range of your products; we think that is not fair, we do not think that you should ask us to do it any longer and we ask you to make it reciprocal. And now it is reciprocal. We have an agreement that upon the list of articles mentioned in that treaty, upon one side or the other, there shall be favoured nation treatment. That is to say, if France shall grant to any country any favour of a commercial character with respect to any one of the items named in that list of our Canadian products, she must also give that advantage to Canada; and, per contra, if we grant any favour to any country as respects the corresponding list on the other side of the treaty, we must also give that to France. That is reciprocity, that is fair. This is an aspect of the question that I would like my hon. friends opposite to understand. I am sure they will see the reasonableness of my argument. While the old treaty remains we are crippled, we cannot negotiate with any .foreign country because any concession that we might grant to any foreign country we would be obliged to give to France for nothing. I think that argument is exceedingly strong; to my mind it is one of the strongest arguments in favour of getting rid of the old treaty and adopting the new one.
Would it not have been perfectly possible for the minister to get rid of the old treaty without making a new one?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and if we got rid of the old treaty we would be in the position that at any time other countries could get an advantage in the markets of France that we could not get. We could have asked the British government to denounce the treaty, and I have no doubt they would have done so, although they would be reluctant to adopt such a course. They would have done so, I have no,doubt, because it is their pride and our pride to recognize tire fact that in all these matters affecting trade, the imperial government desires us to have and exercise the largest possible measure of independence. The freedom which Great Britain now gives us in the negotiation of these treaties is something for which we should all be grateful and proud, and I am sure if we had asked Great Britain to denounce that treaty she would have done so -but would have done so with great reluctance. As was pointed out by one hon. gentleman who spoke yesterday, after years of estrangement France and Great Britain had been brought together and there seemed to be a prospect that they would now work together for their mutual advantage and the promotion of the peace of the world. At such a time it would not have been wise for Canada to have asked for the denunciation of that treaty.

Might I ask the minister if the wine growers in Canada are to have the same advantages as the wine growers in France in regard to the excise on the alcohol that is necessary for the fortification of the wine?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think there has been a misunderstanding. The wine growers were of opinion and represented to us that in France those who produced wine were permitted to take alcohol in bond for the purpose of fortifying their wines, and the wine growers of Canada asked for a similar concession here. I investigated the matter and found that they were mistaken, that the wane growers of France did not enjoy any such advantage. On that point I think the wine growers are now satisfied that they -were mistaken and they are not asking that concession. They are asking a concession of another character which I think is reasonable and which I hope may be granted to them.
What was the nature of that concession?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was- in regard to the use of sugar. If we can make proper customs regulations to guard against abuse,

we are desirous of exempting from duty the sugar which they may use in the production of their wine.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the third time and passed.

["p. TURCOTTE. It is a very simple thing to explain this matter. St. Roch, as hon. gentlemen know is represented by the right hon. the Prime Minister. It was proposed a long time ago to have a public building erected there. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works.) This' amount is required for repairs, and also to build a proper fence around the lower portion of the yard. This is under the Immigration Department.
What is the building worth?

It is a two story brick building on a stone foundation, 115 feet in length by 100 feet in breadth. I do not know the cost of it.
Quebec immigration buildings-additions, renewals, repairs, &c., $6,000.

There was an appropriation for 1909 of $7,500, and there was expended up to the 31st of March, $2,180.95; so that there remains of that vote $5,319.05. It is proposed to spend $2,000 in building a covered way to the building, $595 on the old Marine hospital and $3,419.30 on the immigration buildings generally. This is asked for by the Department of Interior.
Quebee observatory-renewal of water supply pipe, &c., $1,800.
This is asked to make provision for the renewal of 1,200 feet of water-supply pipe which runs from the Grande Allee to the observatory.
What is the size of the pipe?
Three-inch cast-iron pipe. The cost of the pipe is $600 and the cost of the excavation $1 per running foot.
How deep do you go?

Below the frost line, I would suppose five or six feet.
Quebec post office-elevator, improvements, repairs and fittings, $20,000.

This is asked to make provision towards placing an additional story on the head post office building, also to provide an elevator to the ground floor, first and second floors and the attic, also rewiring the building for electric light, and repointing the exterior wail. The total expenditure up to the 31st of October, 1909, was $14,224.62. The estimated cost of rewiring the building is $1,800; raising one story of the extension at the rear, 66 feet Air. FIELDING.
by 35 feet, $12,000; providing for hot water, $1,000; repdinting the extexuor of the building, $5,000; steamfittings, $1,500; contingencies, $1,644. That makes the total cost of the proposed improvements $37,168.62. Then there is the expenditure from 1st April, 1908, to 31st October, 1908, $14,224.62; assumed expenditure to Alarch 31, 1909, $1,794; revote, $7,000; new vote, $13,000. Total, $36,018.62, which still leaves an estimated amount of $1,150 to complete the improvements.
What do you get in the way of space?
We get an additional story on the extension in the rear of 66 feet toy 35. This accommodation is very much required by both the Post Office Department and the Customs.
Do you get any other extension besides that rear extension?
That is the only one. We are also putting an elevator into the building and making quite a number of improvements indicated in the details I have given.
What is the cost of the whole?
Up to the 31st March, $298,000. That of course runs over many years.
It must be in pretty bad state of impairs now. .
It requires considerable repairs.
Is it used for a post office alone?

It is used for post office and customs purposes.
Quebec custom house, $50,000.
How much will it cost?

If we enter upon the construction of a new customs house, that would cost in the vicinity of half a million dollars. If we repair the present customs

house, that will cost between $50,000 and $75,000.

It is very important that we should repair the old house unless we have money to burn. Here you have a customs house, which is pretty well situated, and, although injured by fire, may be repaired at a trifling cost. If the minister can do his work there fairly well, we should consider very carefully before going into an expenditure of half a million dollars because the Harbour Board wants us to do so. There does not seem to be any limit at all to the excursions which the Minister of Public Works is willing to take in the matter of public buildings.

I understood the minister to say that the customs work was done elsewhere and that this building was simply down at the shipping centre for the use of landing waiters. My opinion is that it has no business to be down there. There ought to be a building rented or some other provision made for having that building in another part of the city. I understand the customs house is in connection with the post office.
They use the customs house proper for offices.
This is for a warehouse.
There are customs officials who have offices in the building. The post office is used simply for the postal parcel business in connection with the customs.
What was this place used for which was damaged by fire?

Perhaps I might be allowed to make a few remarks regarding the manner in which the question of removal has come up. Immediately after the fire, which destroyed a very considerable amount of other property, the question occurred to the Transcontinental Commissioners and the Harbour Board whether it would not be desirable to utilize the space burnt over in connection with railway terminal facilities for the Transcontinental. It has been represented to me that, in the opinion both of the Harbour Board and the Transcontinental Commissioners, there is no part of the city which could afford as good opportunities for providing these terminal facilities as this area which has been burnt over. If that part were selected for the terminal facilities, that would necessitate the removal of the customs house to another place. I do not wish to be understood as saying that this site will be given over to the Transcontinental or the Harbour Commission. If they take it, they will have to pay the Department of Public Works what the property is fairly worth. If it should form part of the Transcontinental railway terminal facilities, of course the
Grand Trunk Pacific will pay a rental on the cost. It is a matter of very great importance. It has not yet been decided what we shall do, but it is certainly worthy of most careful consideration.
Does the Minister of Customs require a half million dollar building there?
That matter is with the Public Works Department. I do not know what the building may cost.

Do I understand the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) to say that he abdicates his position entirely with reference to the working of his department in this respect and leaves the matter to the Minister of Public Works? The hon. gentleman (Mr. Paterson) is responsible to the country for the expenditure of his department, and he must have an idea what facilities he requires. Does he want a half million dollar plant, or will a less expensive one do?

I am responsible for the expenditure of my department, but this does not pertain to the expenditure of my department. We have been burned out and must go somewhere. We are temporarily using the present premises, I fear at great inconvenience to the officers. We wished to rent a building there, but the commissioner thought-and his opinion was concurred in by the Public Works Department-that the rent was such that it was not advisable for us to pay it. What we want is to have a custom house in which the business can be properly transacted.
What does the hon. minister think would be a proper provision to give him a .place for his work? Does he think it would cost half a million dollars?
I cannot express an opinion on that.

Then, better let this item stand in the meantime until the Minister of Customs has made up his mind. For I am ready to fight this thing all winter, if necessary, unless we get the views of the Minister of Customs as to what he wants. This method under which the minister whose work is to be done has no wish, desire or plan as to the buildings to be erected for the work of his department, but leaves it entirely with another minister, is one which we have not recognized in this House, This building, if required at all, is required for the work of the Department of Customs. The Minister of Customs, as the head of that department, is the man who ought to requisition the Minister of Public Works for a sufficient building for the service.
That is what we have done.
Then, does the hon. minister agree that an expenditure of half a million will be required?	-
I have not seen either the estimates or the plans.
Then, I think the estimates and the plans had better wait.

I think I can satisfy the hon. member (Mr. Foster). When the estimates were made up and this item of $50,000 put in, the money was intended to repair the custom house building which had been injured by the fire, since that time, we have had this urgent request to remove the custom, house to another site. If we do that, it will necessitate the erection of a new building. In that case, of course, we would sell the present site and building for what they are worth to either the Harbour Commissioners or the Commissioners of the Transcontinental railway. But, before I can properly ask this committee for a vote to erect a new building, I ought to be in a position to state definitely the character of that building and where it is to be erected. Therefore, I would say to the committee that unless we utilize this vote of $50,000 to repair the present custom house we will let the item lapse and come to the House and ask for another annro-priation for the new building.
That is perfectly fair. Now, all we have to look at is the sum of $50,000. Is that sum required to repair the present building?
That is the architect's estimate.
What are the figures in detail?
I have not the details of that estimate before me. But I may say that the attic and half the first floor were completely destroyed.
What was the cost of the building?
If the minister will make it cleaT in the item that this is for repairs, that will make it all right.
Perhaps the committee will take my assurance upon that. I do not feel competent to alter the estimates.
But
Of course, if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) says so, the alteration -can 'be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So long as the amount is not changed, or the meaning destroyed, it can be done.
Then, there is no objection.

speechtext:
The item will read:
Quebec custom house-repairs, $50,000.

This is^ to provide for the completion of the public building now being erected on the corner of St. Joseph and Dorchester streets in Quebec East, frequently spoken of as St. Roch. The building is required for post office purposes.

Yes. The building is to be 49 feet by 48 feet 3 inches; three stories and basement; wall of brick faced with cut stone on the street fronts and stone dressings on the remainder. The cost of heating and boilers will be $2,500; electric wiring and fixtures', $1,- [DOT] 000; fittings, furniture and lock-boxes, $5,000; sidewalks and fences, $1,000; contingencies and superintendence, $8,319. This makes a total estimated cost, including site, of $9,762.50. The total expenditure to October 31, already given, is $43,086; estimated expenditure prior to March 31, 1910, $10,676, so that this vote of $40,000, of which $20,000 is a revote, will make up the entire expenditure.
What was the amount of the contract?
How did the minister get the site, $27,000?
$23,400 was the first payment. The site was valued by arbitrators.
What was the reason for the additional $3,770?
We found, in locating the building, that the lot was not quite large enough, the site would be cramped, and we had to purchase additional land.
What were the dimensions of the first site?

66 feet frontage on the two streets, the lot is 66 feet square. Then it was decided to set the building back a little from the street, and we found there was not space enough in the rear, and we had to buy an addition of 10 feet, I think, in order to give the requisite light.
Does the minister know the revenue of that postal division?

For 1908-9 it was $14,623,60. Money orders issued, $70,692; money orders paid, $7,484. It is a very important division of the city of Quebec. As hon. gentlemen are no doubt aware, by reason of the configuration of the city, there are to all intents and purposes so far as post office requirements are concerned two cities, there is a.n upper city and a lower city. What is the population to be served by that office?
About 40,000.
Does the $47,000 contract cover the heating and wiring?
No, just the building.
Were tenders called for heating, wiring and other matters?
Yes.

Does not the minister think the language of this item is rather indefinite? It says: ' Quebec East, public building'. It does not say whether it is for a post office or not. Does he not think we should specify what the money is required for?

There is only one public building in Quebec East, that is the building under contract. Last session we put in a vote in exactly the same terms, so I do not think it would be desirable to make any change.
I would suggest that you add the words ' post office ' after the words ' public building'.
There is no objection to adding those words.
What is the present cost of the service, and where is it being carried on?
In St. Roch, the rent paid for the post office is $700 per annum, in St. Sauveur, $225. The total is $925. This one building will accommodate both divisions.

The minister said the Postmaster General supported the construction of this building. Is it the custom of the Department of Public Works always to get the support of the Postmaster General before post offices are constructed?
Not always.

Before this building was planned, was there any communication between the Department of Public Works and the Postmaster General as to the nature and kind of building he wanted in which to carry on the post office work?	.
Yes, there were a number of consultations, in which the Postmaster General informed us what was the accommodation required; and plans were submitted to the Post Office Department and approved.
Of course the minister sees what he is doing. Whereas to-day you are paying less than $1,000 for accommodation, the yearly cost of this new building will be close on $10,000.
My hon. friend estimates a 10 per cent basis, I think that is considerably too high.

I do not think so, from 30 years experience. It will come to that.
Mr. BLAIN, How are sites of buildings of this kind selected in the province of Quebec?
'The same as in all the the other provinces of Canada.
In the province of Quebec are sites furnished by municipalities free to the government, or does the gov-ernmept pay for them?

I have not observed any difference in the custom in the province of Quebec from the custom in other provinces. Sometimes the sites are furnished. I can call to mind cases in which sites have been furnished by municipalities in Quebec as well as in other provinces.
What is the rule?
The rule is that the department purchases the sites in all the provinces of Canada.
In St. Catharines, two years ago, the government insisted on the city paying $6,500 for the land before they would erect a public building. That is in Ontario.

That is a matter of agreement. In Quebec there are large numbers of public buildings constructed on sites which are purchased by the Crown. I have now in mind Shawenegan Falls, in

the province of Quebec, where the county and the municipality furnished the site free. In Iberville I think the same way. I have never found that there is any difference between one province and another in that respect. Occasionally sites are furnished free, but in most cases we have to buy them.
I understand the minister to say that this price was fixed by. arbitration.
Yes.
How are the arbitrators appointed-one by the Department of Public Works and one by the owner of the property?
Yes, and these two generally chose a third.
The property not expropriated but submitted to arbitration?
Yes, and the price agreed upon.
Is the minister able to state that the price fixed by arbitration was greater or smaller than the price offered by the owner?
My recollection is that the owner did not make any offer as to the price he required because he was informed by the department that it would be necessary to fix the value by arbitration.
Who were the arbitrators? The minister having in mind the fact that they were very able men should remember the names.

I satisfied myself that the department was represented by a thoroughly competent and reliable man, but I cannot at present give my hon. friend the name because I have no memorandum of it. I -would have no objection at all to submitting the name later on.

The reason I ask the minister if there is any difference in the selection of sites in the province of Quebec and other provinces is. on account of an article that I haye before me from the province of Ontario. It says:
Pergus post office-Liberals hold meeting to decide on. the site.
Pergus, Dec. 1.-A public meeting of local Liberals was held to-night for the purpose of recommending to the government a site for the proposed post office. Four sites were voted upon, the final vote giving the Monroe property a majority of six over the Watt property.
It seems to be the policy at Fergus in Ontario, that when a site is to be selected the Liberals are called together, the different sites are submitted and voted upon, and I suppose that the policy will be that the Mr. iPUGSLLY.
majority shall rule. I want to know whether the same policy is applied in Quebec and other provinces or whether the minister is going to abolish this in favour of the new policy which he is introducing.

There is no policy in Ontario, or any other province, by which we accept the recommendation of the Liberal committee or of anybody else in the locality as to the selection of a site. Of course, we cannot nrevent people in a locality, no matter what political party they belong to, making a recommendation as to what, in their judgment, would be the best site for a public building. But we do in every case send one of our own officials to make an examination of the site, to compare the price at which one site can be obtained with that asked for other eligible sites and to make his report and recommendation as to which in his judgment is most desirable for the public building. In the case of Fergus we sent a very experienced representative of the department^ to that town and it was upon his examination and report that the purchase of the property was made.
Would my hon. friend state to the committee which of these properties was selected?
We will come to that when we reach the Ontario items, and I would ask my hon. friend to wait.
I am quite willing, only T want to give a note of warning to my hon. friend.
I will have the information.
I hope my hon. friend will state whether it was the Munro site or the Watt site.
Yes, I will.

I will not say that. My hon. friend will see the reason. It might very well be that when our representative goes into a locality he naturally confers with the most intelligent, the most influential and the most disinterested people, and he would get their views.

That makes the work easier.
Yes, it makes it easier and very much cheaper for my hon. friend.

At what price per foot?
